newsitem.title: FRANCE: Guillen, Bernard tipped for Bank of France posts.
newsitem.headline: Guillen, Bernard tipped for Bank of France posts.

text.p: The French government was expected on Friday to name two new members to the Bank of France's key policy council in a move which could shift the bias towards faster interest rate cuts, French newspapers said.

Dailies Liberation and Le Figaro said that Pierre Guillen, ex-head of the employers federation CNPF, and Jean-Rene Bernard, former deputy governor at property lender Credit Foncier, were the favourites to fill two posts falling vacant next week.
The government was due to make a decision at a cabinet meeting.
They would replace ex-journalist Jean Boissonnat and former banker Bruno de Maulde on the independent central bank's nine-member monetary policy council.

Officials at President Jacques Chirac's office have declined all comment on the nominations. But one source close to the nomination process said on Thursday the government could choose Guillen and Bernard.

Other sources had said previously that Chirac had intervened personally to get Guillen and Bernard on the list of six nominees proposed by the heads of the upper and lower houses of parliament and the advisory Economic and Social Council.

Daily Les Echos said on Friday, however, that Boissonnat, who is seeking to stay on, might still be in the running, while Liberation said there might still be a last minute change in favour of the former financial journalist.
His reappointment would reassure financial markets worried about any softening in the bank's commitment to defending the stability of the franc against the mark.
Afternoon daily Le Monde said last week the Bank of France, which gives an opinion in a purely advisory capacity, had recommended Boissonnat, who is seeking to stay on, and Bernard.

Boissonnat and de Maulde are believed to be part of a six to three majority backing the existing policy of maintaining French interest rates slightly above those in Germany to protect the stability of the franc against the mark.

Two others members have argued publicly that France should cut rates without waiting for German easing to revive the economy and help bring down record 12.7 percent unemployment. A third member is believed to share that view.
Sources close to the nomination process have said Guillen and Bernard could support this approach.

But whatever the decision, Chirac, who has repeatedly stated his commitment to a stable currency, is seen as unlikely to do anything to endanger the franc-mark link, the cornerstone of the future European single currency.
If Chirac named Guillen and Bernard, it would probably be on the understanding no risks were to be taken with the franc.
The nomination of Guillen and Bernard, ousting Boissonnat, a vocal supporter of the stable franc policy, would nonetheless give Chirac big leverage over the Bank of France.
In an interview with Reuters last month, Guillen, 69, said he was "radically against" devaluing the franc but, as an industrialist, would like to have seen rates fall faster.

Bernard, 64, whose son-in-law is deputy secretary-general in Chirac's office, is not thought to have any very strong convictions on monetary policy. But he is close to Chirac and would be expected to follow the president's lead on policy.

The other candidates on the list of nominees are diplomat Pierre Achard, Alain Prate, former vice-president of the European Investment Bank (EIB), and Robert Pelletier, former managing director of the Association of Credit Establishments (Afec), sources close to the nomination process have said.
